title: How To Get Students To Stay Seated And Quiet In Time-Out et-in-time-out/
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Prompted by a reader question about a kindergartner who crawled under tables during time-out, Linsin explains why a student misbehaving during time-out is a warning sign that the consequence itself isn't working. He lays out six corrective steps: modeling the entire time-out procedure in detail, explicitly teaching students what not to do based on observed misbehavior, having students practice and demonstrate the procedure, keeping engaging activities in reserve to make time-out a genuine loss, backing time-out with an additional consequence tied to something students especially value, and following through consistently every time. He advises against reacting in the moment to a student misbehaving in time-out, instead waiting until the student has settled before calmly delivering the added consequence. The piece frames this combination of interest-building and unbending accountability as the winning formula for effective classroom management.
points: A student misbehaving inside time-out signals that the consequence itself isn't currently effective and needs reinforcement.
Detailed modeling and practiced demonstration of the time-out procedure prevent confusion about expectations.
Time-out only works if students feel they are genuinely missing something they value, which requires deliberately building engaging classroom activities.
Reacting in the moment to time-out misbehavior (yelling, lecturing) backfires; wait until the student settles, then calmly deliver a follow-up consequence.
quotes: When a student misbehaves in time-out, it’s a blinking sign that your time-out isn’t working and won’t effectively curb misbehavior. Furthermore, it’s an act of defiance and shows a lack of concern over your consequences.
Show your students a complete picture, from start to finish, of what they're expected to do if told to go to time out. Use detailed modeling.
Time-out is only effective if the student feels he or she is missing something.
If you try to “win the battle” by yelling, demanding, or lecturing, you’ll lose the war (so to speak).

As you increase the interest, excitement, and enjoyment in your classroom, as well as your likability, classroom management becomes an easier proposition. Add to it an unbending commitment to accountability, and you have an unbeatable combination.
